summary: A town of just over 5,300 people where the median home costs nearly $2 million — roughly 12.4 times the median household income of $158,218 — St. Helena sits on the narrow floor of the Napa Valley, hemmed between the Mayacamas range to the west and the Vaca Mountains to the east, giving even a short evening walk the backdrop of vine-striped hillsides catching golden hour light. The economy is overwhelmingly tethered to wine: vineyards, tasting rooms, and hospitality constitute the bulk of local employment, which means switching jobs without a commute usually means switching to another winery or restaurant rather than another industry. Main Street is genuinely walkable and lined with tasting rooms, independent restaurants, and specialty food shops — not a chain-dominated strip — but the town's 5.1 square miles and low density (about 1,050 people per square mile) mean that once you step off that commercial spine, you're quickly in quiet residential streets or open vineyard land. Climate is generous: averaging 9.3 hours of sunshine daily, warm dry summers pushing highs into the upper 80s, and mild winters rarely dipping below the mid-30s at night — fog is more a Carneros and southern Napa phenomenon, so St. Helena gets more consistent warmth. Rent at $2,391 a month looks almost modest next to those purchase prices, underscoring a sharp buy-versus-rent gap that the local, largely hospitality-driven wage structure below the median would strain to bridge. At its core, St. Helena is a five-square-mile agricultural company town that happens to produce one of the world's most expensive crops — and the real estate is priced accordingly.
